title: Heart Sutra, Part 6: Empty Marks, Empty Chains
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reflects on the wisdom of the Heart Sutra, which teaches that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence and marked by impermanence, helping us let go of attachments and find freedom from suffering. This understanding can help us see through our limited views and perceptions, recognizing that everything is interconnected and not separate from ourselves or each other. By embracing this emptiness, we can cultivate a deeper understanding of reality and begin to heal the mind.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Thanks for handling that Aidan.
Good to see everybody.
Here we are.
How interesting that a group of us could choose to spend our evening this way, huh?
Doing absolutely nothing productive, stopping, listening to our hearts, listening to the talk, listening to our breath, listening to our crazy minds.
How great.
For those of you who haven't been on Wednesday night in a while, we've been slowly meandering our way through the chant we just chanted, the Heart Sutra.
It's a central wisdom teaching in the Zen school that's recited pretty much at all important occasions and at all regular practices in Zen places all over the world.
And on Monday we also chanted it at Bayview Cemetery, which is a large cemetery in town next to Wacom Falls Park.
It's worth exploring there if you've never been in there.
We focus on the city of the living, which we should also visit the city of the dead.
A group of us chanted it there at Luba Pekishiva's funeral on Monday.
We had some remembrances of Luba.
Probably many of you didn't have the opportunity to meet her.
She was a very quiet and unassuming person.
She was quite devoted to our hiking program.
At the funeral, we found out some of the other things she was devoted to because she didn't really talk about herself that much.
So there were people from other walks of life who one by one all said basically the same thing.
They said, "Oh, I didn't know she was into this other thing," each other thing.
So I thought it might be nice to share her obituary written by some of her close friends.
She was 46 years old and passed from salivary cancer.
We remember Luba as a vibrant and sharp yet humble woman, a deep thinker, a radical independent.
She was an avid hiker on the local trails in East Whatcom County and high up in the North Cascades.
She was a diligent advocate for justice, ecological conservation, and against oppressive systems.

She met many of her friends on outdoor excursions along the Mount Baker Highway, up in the woods, on trails, in activist circles, or in Bellingham, where she would frequent the community food co-op Trader Joe's and other local spaces, including community spiritual outlets.
I don't know why they said outlets.
That's kind of great.
Spiritual outlets that she enthusiastically participated in, such as Shir Ha Shalom, Jewish Renewal, and Red Suiters End Community.
Luba was a medical interpreter by profession and had a knack for languages and cultures.
Born in Ostrakan, which is in Siberia, Russia, she emigrated to the United States with her mother as a teenager.
She was fluent in Russian and English and liked learning words and ideas from various traditions, here and far, near and far.
She was well versed and well read in mythology, history, and current events from around the globe.
She graduated from Portland State with an arts degree and continued to make art throughout her life.
But mostly she found nature to be meditative and healing, and believed in simple living, lived a vegan lifestyle, and was critical of materialistic culture and wasteful practices.
She stood up to protect trees from being cut down for financial or political gain, and loved the natural landscapes of the Pacific Northwest.
She did not go anywhere without her hiking backpack, and she used to go on backpacking trips, which she loved.

In her words, *the act of moving through nature quietly, attentively, propelling yourself forward by your breath and muscles balances and quiets the mind, opening it to a sense of contentment and awe.* Shortly before she entered hospice care, Luba said she had a lot left to do in her life.
There were places she hoped to be able to hike during her lifetime.
In honor of Luba, you may want to plant or protect a tree or go on a hike in a beautiful place.
We always remember how Luba loved her cats with such tenderness, found refuge in nature, held strong values and advocated for them, and participated with us in events, hikes and gatherings.
She's leaving behind a legacy of activism, kindness, and simplicity, and she's survived by her mother, Galina.

The detail they chose not to put in the obituary is she lived in a very simple home in the woods in Kendall, and in between the small little places, even though it was a quite simple, low income community, the original developers had left little green belts, pretty small little green belts in between the parcels.
I don't know if they had to, but maybe they just did it out of goodness.
So small little plots and small little green belts.
One day, Luba heard a weird, loud noise, the chainsaw.
She looked out her window and discovered that people were trying to cut down some of the trees in the green belt.
So she confronted them, and they claimed they had permission, but they couldn't prove it, and she didn't believe it.
So she went into her house and waited a little while till they were taking a break, and she snuck out and took their chainsaw and hid it.
I don't forget where she hid it, but they couldn't find it.
As a result of which, she was arrested for theft and spent the next period of her life.
She declined having a public defender.
She wanted to defend herself.
So one of the people that we met at the funeral knew her from the law library.
Then she went to the law library and mastered criminal defense law on her own.
It's quite a long saga defending herself from the loggers.
She was really willing to put herself on the line.
Once I thought about her passing, I thought of a couple other passings of dear Zen friends, so I want to share a couple more remembrances.
A second Zen friend who passed in the last few weeks was David Chadwick.
I met David a couple of times.
I remember him visiting Bellingham once, probably for a book tour.
I remember driving him to Fairhaven, so maybe we're going to Village Books.
David was an early student of Suzuki Roshi in California.
He was the founding Japanese person of our lineage family, founder of San Francisco Zen Center, where our founding teacher Norman Fischer practiced.
David was one of the early ones.
He came to San Francisco Zen Center as a college dropout in 1966, the year I was born.
He was just 21 years old, and he arrived just in time for a couple months after he got there.
He arrived just in time for the opening of Tosahara Zen Monastery in 1967, which he and his friend Ed Brown were an intimate part of.
Maybe you heard about Ed Brown's famous cookbooks, *Great Zen Cook and Cooke*.
One thing I want to mention about this is it's hard to quite imagine now how thoroughly these folks threw themselves into it.
It was the 60s, for sure, and this Asian spirituality being shared and practiced by Westerners was new, but they just took it so seriously.
It wasn't just like another thing they were going to try out.
They were completely all in, and they were intense about it.
They all moved in.
They didn't just let go on Wednesday.
They were like, "I'm moving in."
They all gave up whatever else they had going on, which was not much, probably, and just jumped in.

Many of them were very serious about Zen, eyes down, often sour expressions, trying really, really hard to be excellent Zen students, a lot of times imitating their Japanese teachers, even falling into kind of talking like them with funny Japanese accents, using Japanese honorifics, calling each other David-san and Ed-san and stuff like that.
David was super into it, but for some reason that didn't stick to him.
He was a lot looser, a little more of a goof-off.
Once they started Tassajara, there were lots and lots of rules.
Someone was just talking to me tonight about how many rules we have around here.
You ain't seen nothing yet, you know?
They had a lot of rules at the monastery, rules governing every aspect of your activity, and rules is maybe an English word we map onto something that's a little bigger than the idea of rules.
Ways of being, ways of practicing, ways of living together in harmony in the community, and yeah, rules.
Anyway, one of the things David would do is he just was interested in people, and they had periods of time where they had visitors to Tassajara who didn't have to follow the rules.
They were paid guests, so the students were working hard, going to the zendo all the time, and doing all the work, and the guests were hanging out and being guests.
One time he got invited into a cabin of some guests.

They had brought their own little barbecue because they had heard it was vegetarian, and they were barbecuing a steak and having whiskey, and they invited, and they invited David, young David, and David was supposed to say, "No, no, no, I really can't," but he didn't.

He said, "Yeah, sure," and then the next morning there was a meeting with the Roshi of all those sort of team heads, and he was the head of the dining hall serving crew, and he staggers in late, obviously hung over, and the other students were so annoyed, you know, and they talked to the Roshi later like, "God, we can't put up with this.
David's just such a goof-off."
And Suzuki Roshi says something like, "David is doing a very good job being David.
Please leave him alone."
But in the end, David Chadwick was really deeply committed to Suzuki Roshi for the rest of his life.

Suzuki Roshi actually died not that many years later in 1971, so yeah, five years after David met him, and just four years since they opened this big monastery, the first Japanese Zen monastery outside of Japan in the world, and they had to figure it out from scratch, you know, how to do all this, and of course, Suzuki Roshi invited Japanese colleagues to help.
It wasn't just the Americans figuring it out, but they basically had to figure it out, and David went on to have a whole other life and do lots of different things.
He did ordain, but he never became a teacher like some of his friends did.

He held it all pretty lightly, but he became, to his surprise, and I think to everyone else's surprise too, he turned out to be a really good writer, and so he spent the rest of his life chronicling the history and writing about his teacher in this early community.
His most well-known book is a biography of Suzuki Roshi called *Crooked Cucumber*, which is really worth reading, which is loving, but also, you know, straight up and fair.

It talks about Suzuki Roshi's big mistakes and failings, as well as his brilliance and insight, and talks honestly about a lot of what happened back then, and you know, depending on your point of view, David was deeply obsessed with those early years or deeply devoted to them or both, so a project he was doing right before he died was a new set of books about Tosahara in the early days, and he managed to get them both done, two books, and the first of which, before he died pretty suddenly from a fast-acting cancer, he narrated it.
So I listened, in the honor of David, I listened to his book, *Tosahara Stories*, read by him, and it's just a delight, maybe more so because I've met him, but I think we'd all enjoy it.

He tells the stories of what happened in that first year at Tosahara, and somehow he got all these details, which I assume are accurate, like exactly what was said in different occasions, like in the big ceremonies where there's formal exchanges and students ask the teacher or the head student questions.
He has them all in there somehow, you know, 50, 60 years later?
Yes, 60 years later, literally, so it's an amazing thing, so bless him for his huge part in showing how this got started here.
You know, you can put yourself right in 1967, thanks to David, and find out how it started.
Down on February 23rd, he was 81 in Bali.
Five, ten years ago, he moved to Bali with his second wife, maybe third wife.

And then the last person I want to memorialize briefly is a Dharma brother of ours, Anka Rick Spencer, who passed away just past midnight early on Monday morning with his dear student, Arhelia, at his side in Mexico City.
Rick was someone I practiced with very intimately for many years.
Chris knew, Anna knew too, several of us knew Rick.
Big, tall, enthusiastic, also a little goofy, I think I just like goofy Zen students the best, you know, but so devoted to practice.
It became his whole life.
He was actually originally from one of the Dakotas, and he fled the U.S. to Canada in the 1960s or early 70s to avoid the draft and prefer the Vietnam War.
I don't know if you know about that, but Canada was pretty welcoming of American draft dodgers for a while.
He did some technology work for the government, for Environment Canada in Vancouver, and then he connected with a Rinzai teacher in Vancouver in 1982, a guy named Eshin.

And then sometime in About the late 1980s or so, he hooked up with a group called the Karuna Meditation Society, which was like Zen and Vipassana and different forms of Buddhism, but a little lighter in spirit maybe than the Rinzai Center.
That group had just started inviting this young teacher named Norman Fischer to start coming to teach with them a couple times a year.
Norman was in his forties then.

After a couple of years with that group and Norman visiting, another group split off, founded partly by Kate McCandless and Michael Newton, who had been in Japan when Rick first was getting interested in Zen.
They came back and formed Mountain Rain Zen Community, which is an important place you can go visit in Vancouver now, a group just like ours.
Rick became a really important part of that group, a central member.
Back in those early days, the Bellingham group was small, and this Vancouver group was small.
We were both groups working with Norman Fischer, and it was a great opportunity for Norman, too, to get to teach more.
In the big Zen Center, he didn't have so many opportunities to teach because he was living at San Francisco Zen Center.
He would come alternately, one time do a retreat in Bellingham, and then a couple of months later do a retreat in Vancouver and back and forth.
At the peak, he was coming six times a year, so literally every couple of months, Norman would be in town.
The group of us would migrate back and forth across the border, which was a little easier to do then.
We really were like one sangha, one international cross-border sangha.
Rick, Kate, Michael, and I kind of became a foursome, and we were the first four that Norman ordained, I think one of us a year for four years straight, from two thousand to two thousand four.
About eight years later, we all four did dharma transmission, also one after the other, and studied together in preparation for that.
We were very, very close, really like siblings.
Rick and I were together for the week of the secret and fabulous and exhausting and fun ceremonies of dharma transmission at Norman Fischer's house, so a very intimate week together there.
He was, as I said, tall, maybe a little awkward, but so sincere, like heartbreakingly sincere.
If you got out of your head and really tuned into him, wanting so deeply to understand the dharma, to really live it, to really be able to share it.
I only recently found out, actually preparing to give this little talk, I found out what his dharma name meant.
I never knew before.

It was Anka Burai, which means dancing thunderbolt, dancing thunderbolt, peaceful transformation, dancing thunderbolt, peaceful transformation, a nice celebration of his energy, dancing thunderbolt, and encouragement towards his growing peacefulness as he went along.
Also during that time, Norman was going south as well as going north from California.
An old friend of his from San Francisco's Zen Center, a Mexican woman, had started a little center in Mexico, so he started going there.
It was a center and a resort and a sort of funding source for social services that she was putting together.
She was a doctor, a deeply, deeply committed woman to social justice.
Norman started doing retreats down there.

Rick went to a couple of those and was so moved by the Mexican sangha, the Mexican culture, Spanish language, that in his late fifties he decided, "I'm going to learn Spanish, retire early, and live in Mexico."
He made that decision one day, maybe in a fit of inspiration at Sachine down there, I don't know.
But unlike many of us, he did it.
He followed through completely.
He was committed to things that way, Rick was.
Within a year or two, he could pretty much teach Zen in Spanish.
To my ear, his accent was a little weird and his cadence was a little strange, but he was fully understandable, clearly.
He quickly gained a huge vocabulary, amazing.
He started a sitting group in Puerto Vallarta, which is near where that center was, and that group thrived for a dozen years or so until it ran out of gas.
Then he and his one close student, Argelia, moved to an apartment in Mexico City, which he called Armita Zen Mexico, Mexico Zen Hermitage, where he lived out the rest of his days.
He also had cancer in his lungs this time.
Goodbye, dear Rick.
Thank you for your beautiful Dharma life.
I'm sorry we didn't stay closer.
As siblings growing up together, we had like some sibling issues, which I think we were over, but we never really got to spend time just enjoying each other once we cleared that up.
I did mean to come to visit you, Rick, in Mexico City, and I'm sorry I didn't prioritize that more.
I really regret that.

Thank you, David Shadwick, for sharing your love and storytelling so we can all be much closer to Suzuki Roshi than we ever could have been without him, and for being so full of yourself from beginning to end.
I do recommend listening to that Tatsuhara Stories book.
He kind of cracks himself up a few times while he's reading it, you know, and all the stuff they got up to.
Does he narrate that too?
Oh, great.
Oh, great.
Yeah.
Quote quoting.
Oh, that's Suzuki Roshi recordings in it.
Oh, so it's more than just reading the book.
Oh, wow.
So Crooked Cucumber, David Shadwick on Audible or audio.
Thanks, hon.
I didn't know that.
It's wonderful.
And thank you, Luba, for sharing your unique Dharma.
I'm glad to share about these people, whether you knew them or not.
It reminds me Norman used to do that.
When someone important to him and someone connected to our practice past, you would tell us about it and remember them.
So it's funny how these things just come around eventually that now I'm old enough to have my Dharma friends and mentors passing away and give talks to the community about it.
So thank you for making that possible.
Somehow this all connects to the Heart Sutra because everything does.
It would be helpful probably to be looking at the text on page five, so we've made it to the third paragraph.
*Shariputra, all dharmas are marked by emptiness.
They neither arise nor cease, nor are they defiled nor pure, nor are they increased nor decreased.* So part of how we think things to be is that they come into being.
They weren't here, and then through some causes or other, they are here.
We recognize that they're here because they have certain qualities that we can recognize and name, right?
This is like, yeah, so, yeah.
And eventually they'll be gone again.
Although our minds seem to work, we seem to lean into the eventually and kind of treat things as sort of temporarily permanent until they're not, right?
We don't have until we have digested the impermanence and change thing.
We know that that is true, and we get along okay seeing the world that way more or less, but we do get stuck right regularly.
We get hung up by things that we don't want coming into being.
That's upsetting, you know.
Then maybe we do lean into impermanence.
"When am I going to get rid of this?" which isn't exactly what it means either.
Or we get hooked on the things that are what we do want, and how do we get more and so on and so forth, and not just material things.
Of course, we're all supposedly too mature to think that material things will make us happy, but we do the same kind of materialism with non-material things, right?
The feelings we want, the kinds of relationships we want, the way things should go.
The emptiness teachings of the Heart Sutra are encouraging us to see through that, that there's something much deeper going on here, more radical, more fluid, and more dynamic.
You would think that emptiness meaning that things are empty of a separate self would actually not be expressed the way this last paragraph expresses it, where it says they don't arise or cease.
You would think the accurate language from the emptiness pundits would be more like constant arising and endless ceasing and incessant increasing and decreasing.
Wasn't that more what they're talking about?
But I guess these great teachers in emptiness must have felt that the problem with that kind of talk is you would still assume that there's some something that's doing the arising and ceasing.
They would only kind of get halfway there.
So to help us, they even refute the idea of arising and ceasing, coming and going.
They're trying to shake us up a little bit here so we can see things in a bigger, broader, deeper way.
This shows up in our ritual life.
We get these little reminders like in our funeral for Luba.
We wanted to offer her infinite, the infinite spaciousness of emptiness.
So we said something like, "In the Dharma world, there's no coming and going."
And even we told her there's no birth and death.
What a wild thing to say at a funeral.

But I think even people who don't know all this Zen stuff, which was the majority of the guests, could somehow feel and appreciate the freedom of that way of looking at it, not being bound by coming and going, birth and death.
There's something in the real openness of the empty nature of everything.
Emptiness is a little bit challenging of a term, but it's, I think, pretty accurate, you know?
There's one, a great little short essay by Dogen called the, basically, the title basically means the acupressure, acupuncture needle of Zen, a very precise little needle.
So emptiness is like an acupressure, acupuncture needle of Zen, and it kind of pokes you, you know?
You might not like it, but maybe it'll open up your energy, like acupuncture does.
The word marked in this little paragraph, "all dharmas are marked by emptiness," is significant all by itself.
This little sutra is full of a zillion references to a huge array of teachings.
So it's also seeking to remind us of the depth and breadth of Buddha's teachings, even as it reminds us further that they're all empty.
To say that they're empty does not mean they're no good or something.
Although, yeah, see, the needle's a little tricky.
No, it means they're even better than you thought.
They're absolutely true, and they're not true at all.
They're beyond true and untrue.
The word marked points to an early Buddha's teaching called the three marks of existence.

It's a really useful, important teaching, which is to reflect on the truth that every moment of existence, every moment of experience, which sometimes they call every dharma with a little d when it's translated in English, every dharma, every like piece, every like moment, is actually marked by three things, like it or not.
The three things are impermanence, not-self, and dukkha, or suffering, it's usually translated, but we'll get to that.
This is another kind of acupuncture needle, like that doesn't sound great, you know, right?
"Every moment of existence is impermanent, non-self, and suffering."
My standard joke, which seems to be really applicable all the time in these talks, is like, no wonder Zen groups are small, right?

You got to sort of get through the initial shock of this kind of challenging language to realize the grace and beauty of it all, you know, and how helpful it is to let go of trying to find things that are all, you know, just the way you want them.
So anyway, let's go through these and maybe it'll make sense with a little bit of explanation why this is useful and helpful and actually quite beautiful.
The first mark of impermanence we already talked about, and it's simple and nobody could argue with it, you know, and yet really appreciating it as a lifetime of practice.

I think mostly the way I practice with impermanence, and maybe you do too, is noticing the suffering that comes very reliably when I forget about impermanence, when I try to deny impermanence, when I try to don't act really in accord with the truth of impermanence, when I try to fix things in place, you name it, you know, internal, external, doesn't matter.
So impermanence is a path to freedom for sure, because when we don't, when we're out of harmony with impermanence, we suffer.
When we're in harmony with impermanence, we don't.

It's deeply connected to the second mark of all experience is that everything is not me, you know, is not self or non-self, which is pretty similar to what we talked about before in the earlier paragraphs about the five aggregates about the way we mistake everything for me, me, me, but actually it's really just a collection of experiences that maybe fit in these categories like form and perception and so on.
So this is another way of looking at that without needing to put things in categories: that nothing is exactly me, including the things that I think are me.
It's easy to think the wall over there is not me, but then you have some great idea or some troubling idea, and without thinking about it, you think that's me, right?
We do that, and so we're stuck in our vision of me-ness, which again, non-emptiness gets us pretty far.
We do okay; it can function, but I think we wouldn't be here if that really was enough.

We somehow intuit there's something more to this than trying to make me into me—better me, defend me, terrible me, good—all the incredible amounts of energy we all put into me-maintenance, or resisting me-maintenance or whatever your pattern is, me-denial.
This is not denial of me; it's freedom in me and beyond me, so that every moment experience is not me.
And yes, this third mark does sound the most troubling, although not me can be a little challenging too, right?
Because we're used to me and we're kind of comfortable in our kind of messy me.
If we took away all the me, what would be left?
But the third one is the most challenging sounding one, that all moments of experience are marked with dukkha, which is usually translated as suffering.
But suffering is not such a great translation; it's okay, but it doesn't get the subtlety of the term, the original term, which is a Sanskrit word similar in Pali.
So dukkha is about the challenge we inevitably experience when we try to get lasting satisfaction from things that just aren't going to give us that satisfaction, including number one, me.
And so that seems like that does tie into the previous one pretty well.
But also another aspect of dukkha is the way we are distressed and suffer when there's something that changes that we don't want it to change, which is like everything; we don't like change, right?
And that's back to the first one, right, impermanence.
So they're really working together here, supporting each other and helping to free us, helping to free us.
And this whole process of constantly being me is just all kinds of dukkha, right?
So it all fits together.

Not to say there aren't appearances and experiences, and we do have a sense of our separateness, but we start to feel and understand at all levels that our separateness is more of a mirage, a useful mirage than anything else.
Useful when it's useful, sometimes not useful at all.
I probably mentioned a couple of times the really great metaphor of the wave on the ocean: that if you just think you're the wave, that's the separate self, right?
But you look down, you remember we're all the same ocean, we're all the same aliveness, we're all the same beingness, that we are empty of separateness completely.
It's a convincing illusion, isn't it?
We believe in it, but there are also moments when you're not so sure.
Have you had those moments?
These are so encouraging.
Someone was just talking to me about hallucinogenic stuff, and I think that's part of why there seems to be some overlap in that and what we're doing here, that can help us soften the boundaries.
But practice itself softens the boundaries just fine.
Little by little, sometimes you experience it a little more in fits and starts, but little by little, we're all opening to these truths whether we consciously know it or not.
*Shariputra, all dharmas are marked by emptiness, they neither arise nor cease, are neither defiled nor pure, neither increase nor decrease.*
Want to hang in there for one more paragraph?
You okay?
We're good?
All right.
You're not really here anyway, so I'll just keep talking, but I'm not either, so.
Okay, then it says, now we have the famous no, no, no, no, no, no.
How come at the end of the evening when we're saying good night, thanks for coming, half the people aren't like, what's with this no, no, no thing?
That's like weird, you know?
Why do you have us chant that?
I don't know why we never get that objection; everyone's just too nice or something.
Or maybe you intuited emptiness so deeply you didn't need to ask.
It's kind of strange though, so let's read this next paragraph.

*Therefore, given emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, no perception, no formation, no consciousness, no eyes, no ears, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind, no sight, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, no object of mind, no realm of sight, no realm of mind, consciousness.*
The dot, dot, dot in there for some reason.
So at one point I was wondering, is this even translated right?
No, no, no, no.
So I checked it out, and yeah, it is.
In Sanskrit they use the word na, which means no.
Where we have no form, no feeling.
They have na rupam, na vedana.
So it's the same.
The Chinese uses the little character wu or mu, most famous character in the Zen world for sure.
It looks like a little kind of a gate, kind of like this.
Yeah, actually it's really pretty close to that.
It's like a gate you can't get through; it's the word for no.
So that's what's used in the Chinese translation, which we then chant in Sino-Japanese as mu this, mu that, mu, mu, mu, mu, mu, mu, mu, same thing.
So this is strange sounding because we do appear to have eyes.

There's a famous story I meant to look it up because I couldn't remember exactly who said this; I'm not going to guess because I'm going to get it wrong, but there was an early Zen master as a child who one time heard this sutra and was courageous enough to pipe up to the great master and say, "I have eyes."
And of course this led eventually to their lifelong practice and awakening and becoming a great master themselves.
So what's this saying?
It's not saying no exactly; that's just a convention they use because this is also a very kind of dense and efficient text, no extra words, you know.
They're saying no, your eyes aren't exactly the eyes you think they are, and the way they show you sights aren't exactly the sights that you think they are.
And who's doing the thinking?

Your sight consciousness, your eye consciousness, which here gets translated as realm, your realm of sight, is interpreting, is limited, is not seeing the whole reality because we're not fully understanding and living in harmony with the empty nature of all that is.
So it's a great encouragement to look again, to look more carefully, to listen more carefully, to look more deeply.
Dogen's always talking about this too, like study this carefully, look more deeply.
So it's an encouragement to us to not be sure about the appearances being the whole thing.
And you experience this in practical ways like in relationships and stuff, right?
The first you're just seeing somebody's appearance and you immediately form a dozen judgments, right?
Or a hundred judgments or a thousand judgments about what the person's about and where they're from and what they're good at and blah, blah, blah, you know.
But then you get to know them, right?
And you see, oh, there's a lot more to this person than I thought, right?
You still don't really know them, right?
This is an infinite process.
So the no is renouncing limited views, limited thoughts, limited understandings with all five senses and the mind.
That's what the no means.
And it's following here first the five skandhas that we've already looked at multiple times, right?

So they really made that point strongly, like three times over in this small text told us how truly empty the skandhas are, these aggregates that we think of as ourselves, that we have experiences of form, of preference, of perception, of thoughts and mental patterns, and that's all they are, you know, they're not you.
